Does your Steam demo CCU ‘predict’ your game’s success?
We’ve got data. Unsurprisingly. Also: lots of news & new GameDiscoverCo Show.
Simon Carless
Sep 09, 2026
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
We’re right back at it, and we’re wondering how y’all doing out there. Reasonable? OK? Hunky dory? We’re… how do you say… rather excited to get on with our job, which is providing you much info on why video games are popular. So we’ll do that!
Before we start, the runaway ‘silly story’ intro slot winner this week: “ Elden Ring Director Hidetaka Miyazaki Says He’s ‘Honestly Not Sure’ Where the Rumor About Him Having a Foot Fetish Came From .” Good job, IGN (and The Guardian for doing The Duskbloods interview .) So no, plz don’t call Miyazaki ‘ Tarantino-esque’ …
[ NEED THE BEST DATA? You can get a free demo of our GameDiscoverCo Pro company-wide ‘Steam deep dive’ & console data, inc. MCP server, by reaching out today - >110 orgs have it. Or, signing up to GDCo Plus gets extra newsletter and Discord access, plus more .]
Game discovery news: summon the Wardogs…
Let’s take a look at some of the more notable game platform & discovery news since late last week, as follows:
Here's GDCo Pro estimates of 'trending' unreleased Steam games by 'new wishlists in the last 7 days' , Sept 1st-7th - and 'friendslop in the air' standout Dear Passengers (#1) and tactical shooter Wardogs (#3) shouldn’t be a surprise (We’ve talked less about F2P ARPG creature collector Aniimo (#2), which has good momentum.)
At #4, The Missing Tail , from Estoty (creators of VR/mobile hit I Am Cat ) does the 'two player co-op only' thing with cozy cat shenanigans, getting ~100k wishlists in no time. And PlayStation's State Of Play helped Final Fantasy VII Revelation (#5) and FF: Resonance (#9), as well as killer shark sequel Maneater 2 (#8) trend.
According to data provided to The Game Business , “The GTA 6 Netflix reveal has caused a spike in sales of PlayStation and Xbox hardware. According to Nielsen IQ, UK PS5 sales jumped 33% [in the week following the reveal], while Xbox Series S and X sales leapt 34%.” The public, they love grand theft-ing in their autos…
Over on Facebook (!) former Epic wunderkind Cliff Bleszinski has views on the ‘Crash 2.0 for games ’ rhetoric: “So is the end near? Hardly. ‘Life finds a way”’ - keep looking towards the AA/’slop’ area to find the fun, and at a reasonable price, which allows you to sample a bunch of quirky, innovative titles with friends. Let AAA faceplant for a while, I say.”
Spotting smaller Steam games getting more front page referrer traffic than they used to? That’s cos, some time recently, Valve changed the featured front-page games in ‘ Discounts & Events ’ (the non-Daily Deal ones) to be more personalized to logged-in player interests. (A good move to help the little guys, done quietly.)
Here’s a fun site, PS Store DB , which is scraping all PlayStation Store game ratings and creating a ‘Highest Rated weighted by review count’ score. For games with >10k reviews, the top games are Dispatch (4.93/5), Persona 5 Royal (4.91/5), the OG Final Fantasy VII (4.9/5) and Persona 4 Golden (4.9/5), among others…
We don’t talk about AI much, but Nvidia’s DLSS 5 ‘lighting diffusion model’, now shipping in NBA 2K27, is prob. the highest-profile incursion into games so far. There’s a ResetEra thread summarizing a longform Digital Foundry video we found v.helpful: “DLSS 5 best suited for games that are trying to look realistic.”
As passed along by RoadToVR : “Valve has pushed an update to the Steam Link PC VR streaming app on Quest that finally includes the ability to play games via wired connection.” Why now? One commenter notes: “Meta only recently added support for video over USB , and Steam Link could not have implemented wired support without it.”
Errata: on Friday’s August charts we noted that puzzle co-op hit Big Walk had 3m+ PlayStation players (and more downloaders) due to it launching as a PlayStation Plus ‘monthly game’ . But looks like 99%+ of those (not 90%, as we put in the charts) are from PS+ players. (We’ll keep tweaking our PS+ download splits.)
Microlinks: Xbox tells existing Game Pass members its new cloud gaming cap doesn’t apply to them , but only in certain countries; Apple may be working on first-party game controllers ; if you dropped Xbox Game Pass, MS may try to tempt you back with a personal discount price (as low as $16/month for Ultimate.)

Does your Steam demo CCU ‘predict’ outcomes?
How did these titles ‘convert’ their demo CCU? Let’s find out…
Headline: in this era when more Steam games are using pre-release demos to gauge interest & get feedback, we realized: we didn’t formally study the relationship between demo CCU and game CCU . But we can, thx to GameDiscoverCo Pro data (we have concurrents hourly from 2024 & just acquired daily peak CCU back to 2018.)
Firstly, some context: we checked the top 100 top-grossing games of 2026 so far on Steam , and found that 58 of them had a pre-release demo . That includes only 6 of the Top 20 (inc. Windrose, Pragmata) but three quarters (15) of those ranked #81-#100. So when you get below Forza & 007-sized games, it’s extremely common.
Let’s go for a high-level visualization to start. If your game’s demo got more than 50 concurrents on Steam, what was the peak-all time CCU of your game? Well, the median was 3.01x , and here’s the various ranges:
This, we think, is genuinely useful new info, calculated from the 2,569 Steam games we found that launched between Jan. 2024 and Aug. 2026 with a >50 CCU demo . (There were about 55,000 games launched in that time, so that’s only 4.7% of all games.)
So here’s how to think about this 3.01x multiplier - or at least, how we think about it:
Let’s say your game’s demo got 200 CCU on Steam: this means, at median, you might see the full version launch to 600 CCU, which very roughly translates to (if not a pre-orderable game!) about ~12,000 units sold Week 1, and 35,000 units Year 1.
But there’s a lot of moving parts here, both up and down: it’s hardly a fixed ratio! The top 20-30% of demos convert to peak game CCU at 6.24x, and the bottom 20-30% at 1.29x. That’s a 4-5 times difference, pretty quickly. The median isn’t gospel.
Nonetheless, these ratios are important for understanding probability: let’s say your game had a 100 CCU demo, and you need to sell 100k copies in your first year on Steam. To do that, you may need a 16x ‘demo→game’ multiplier.
Is a 16x multiplier (from peak demo CCU to peak game CCU) doable? Absolutely! But you’d need to be in the top 10% of ‘demo to game’ CCU conversion for it to happen. And you need to have a compelling reason why your game would perform that well. (Was the demo underpromoted? Will the main game somehow go more viral?)
Anyhow, we picked out select games with particularly high, near-median, and below-median performance of peak demo to peak game CCU, and here they are:
The high-converters? Mainly games like Megabonk and Escape From Duckov with incredibly strong hook or game design loop that had good interest pre-release (demo CCUs in the hundreds or low thousands), but hit giant CCU highs post-release.
It’s notable there’s not much friendslop in here - partly because friendslop is so inexpensive that it often just launches without a demo? But there’s some co-optional titles that grew over time like Abiotic Factor & LORT, as well as just straight out great ‘sleeper/breakout’ hits like Absolum , Moonlight Peaks , and even Dispatch .
We also wanted to show a range of titles that were closer to ‘normal’ - including solo indie hits like Road To Vostok (3.3x) and AA-ier rhythm action title Dead As Disco (2.34x). If we were using this data to mentally model for your game, we’d probably use 2x-4x as a starting point…
Finally, here’s some games that had stronger demo performance in CCUs than full game performance. (Sorry if you’re featured!) It looks like some of these like Drive Together or Ghostbane are very strong hook for casual demo players, but ‘execution-light’ at commercial release.
Some of the other titles had PR/marketing firepower aimed at the demo rollout, or tried to charge above what the market thinks acceptable for certain styles of game. ($5-$15 is increasingly the norm?) That’s the rough shape of it - please ping us if you see any data discrepancies btw, because we can’t manually check >2,500 games easily.
Finally, we showed this early data to someone who wondered how the median differs, depending on the CCU cut-off. Good question, and the median ‘demo → game’ peak CCU multipliers are like this for demo concurrents: >10 CCU = 2.40x, >50 CCU = 3.01x, >100 CCU = 2.91x, >250 CCU = 2.59x, >500 CCU = 2.41x, >1000 CCU = 2.38x .
(So: as the demo CCUs get bigger, the multiplier and spread gets somewhat smaller, as outliers are removed. Makes total sense to us…)
GameDiscoverCo Show: backing off multiplatform
Finally and ultimately, we’re back with The GameDiscover Show , ft. myself (Simon) and Post Games’ Chris Plante with a bunch of extra insight - sub to the podcast via Apple Music , Spotify & elsewhere (audio), with a video version on YouTube (above).
On this episode, we talk about how PC game hardware increases might also stretch the game biz in similar ways to console & discuss how Xbox and PlayStation are in some ways getting 'less multiplatform' . We also look at some good points from Arrowhead's CEO and talk about why that Xbox cloud limitation (maybe!) happened.
[ We’re GameDiscoverCo , an analysis firm based around one simple issue: how do players find, buy and enjoy your PC or console game? We run the newsletter you’re reading, and provide real-time data services for publishers, funds, and other smart game industry folks.]

title: Just Dessert vs. Gossip Harbour: Who Merged It Better?
author: Aylin Yazıcı
excerpt: Deconstruction of Gossip Harbour vs Just Dessert
text:
Written by Yael Halevi , aka Merge Queen and casual games strategist, bringing you insights shaped by years of professional Game Design experience and learnings from smash merge hits like Travel Town.
For years, I’ve been following the gaming industry, and one of my favorite things to track is new game releases.
New games do more than just introduce new competitors. They often predict future trends, bring innovation, and show off creative mechanics. Most importantly, they give me insights into what the "next big thing" might be.
I invite you to follow me here! I’ll be sharing bite-sized, insightful posts about interesting new games, why they matter, and my personal take on them.This past May brought us several intriguing titles. However, one that truly stands out is Just Desserts , a new soft-launch title from Chinese gaming giant Century Games , better known for the most successful strategy games, Whiteout Survivals & Kingshot.
Merge 2 Crash Course
For those unfamiliar with the Merge genre, here is a quick catch-up: this genre has skyrocketed in popularity over the last few years, becoming the 2nd highest-grossing in the casual genre after match-3. Furthermore, it has shown phenomenal year-over-year growth, and it’s not slowing down anytime soon.
Right now, the undisputed king of the genre is Gossip Harbor (from Chinese Microfun ), which has comfortably cemented its spot as one of the Top 5 highest-grossing mobile games globally.
To give you a quick, no-nonsense crash course on how we got here: Gossip Harbor actually started as a game heavily inspired by Love & Pies (from Trailmix, a Supercell studio). But in a classic student-surpasses-the-master twist, it outworked and evolved into a fierce competitor that has left everyone else in the dust.
But market growth alone doesn’t explain why Merge 2 has become such a powerful genre. To understand what makes these games so engaging, and why the formula has proven so scalable, we need to look under the hood at the core gameplay loop that drives the experience.
The Core Gameplay Loop
The core gameplay loop takes place on a board filled with Producers and orders that give players clear goals to work toward. Players tap Producers to generate items, then merge two items of the same type to progressively reach the items required by orders. Each tap consumes Energy, making it the resource that powers the core loop.Completing these orders rewards players with resources, enables progression, and ultimately allows them to renovate and develop the Meta, the space where the game’s narrative unfolds.
While the board provides the moment-to-moment gameplay, the Meta and its narrative give that gameplay a larger purpose. Players are not simply merging items for the sake of merging, they are completing orders for the characters they have become invested in, using their progress to unlock new areas, advance the story, and see what happens next.The interesting part is that the merge loop doesn’t exist in isolation. While the board provides the actions that keep players busy, the Meta gives those actions meaning. This connection between gameplay and narrative is one of the key reasons Merge 2 games can turn a relatively simple mechanic into such a sticky experience.
Narrative as a Retention Driver
Narrative plays a critical role in the overall experience and is one of the key drivers bringing players back to the game. This is particularly relevant in the Merge 2 genre, where the majority of the audience is female and emotional investment in characters can become a powerful engagement driver.
Love & Pies is one of the strongest examples of this approach. The game established a highly engaging cast of distinctive characters and built a compelling narrative around them, helping it achieve exceptionally strong retention within the genre. Its approach to character-driven storytelling has since become an important benchmark for many Merge 2 titles that followed, including Gossip Harbor .
Importantly, the narrative characters are not disconnected from the core gameplay. They are also the characters requesting orders on the board. This creates a direct relationship between the two layers of the game: the characters provide the motivation, while the board provides the activity through which players help them. Players are effectively “working for” these characters, transforming each merge and completed order into a small contribution toward the larger story.
The “One More Merge” Effect
A major part of what makes the Merge 2 loop so compelling is the perception of constant, achievable progress .
Every order is broken down into smaller merging steps, creating a clear path toward completion. As players get closer to the requested item, the goal feels increasingly attainable- often creating the feeling that they are “just one more merge” away.
This creates a powerful progression illusion: the player is continuously moving forward, but there is always another small step within reach. That combination of visible progress, achievable goals, and incomplete tasks makes disengagement surprisingly difficult.
The board itself reinforces this behavior. Players are constantly balancing several micro-goals at once as they find themselves caught in an almost endless OCD-like loop: generating items, merging, completing orders, freeing up board space, and organizing their inventory. This creates a highly satisfying optimization loop in which players naturally want to “clean up” the board before stopping.
In other words, the game is not only asking players to progress,it is constantly giving them something that feels almost finished.
Energy: The Resource Powering the Economy
At the center of the game economy is Energy , the primary resource governing item generation.
Players spend Energy by tapping Producers, with one tap costing one Energy . This creates a direct relationship between the core gameplay action and the game’s primary resource economy: the more players want to merge and progress, the more Energy they need to generate items.
Energy regenerates automatically at a rate of one Energy every two minutes , with a maximum capacity of 100 Energy . As a result, a fully depleted player can naturally refill their Energy in approximately 3 hours and 20 minutes .
This creates a built-in return loop . Players who want to maximize their free Energy have a clear incentive to return several times throughout the day, turning resource regeneration into a lightweight but effective retention mechanism.
Energy as a Monetization Lever
Energy not only regulates gameplay, but it also creates one of the game’s most important monetization opportunities.
Once players run out of Energy, they are presented with the option to purchase additional Energy using Gems. The cost increases with successive purchases, starting at 10 Gems , followed by 20 Gems , then 40 Gems , and so on. Importantly, the Energy purchase ladder resets daily, making it more than a one-off monetization opportunity: it becomes part of the player’s daily resource routine.
Personally, I find this to be one of the game’s more powerful “slippery slope” monetization areas. The individual purchases feel small and easy to justify; 10, 20, or even 40 Gems can feel like such a low commitment that I barely register them as a meaningful purchase. Yet because the ladder resets every day, these small decisions can quickly become part of my daily routine.
This is one of the few games where I genuinely feel that I have very little resistance to making these small, recurring purchases. The game almost smoothly and subtly nudges me into spending, without any single purchase feeling significant enough to trigger a strong sense of friction. This is a strong example of the foot-in-the-door effect: the first, relatively small purchase lowers the psychological barrier to spending, making the next purchase feel more acceptable, and so on.
That makes the Energy system particularly interesting from a monetization perspective: the strength is not necessarily in the size of the purchase, but in how effortlessly the game turns spending into a habit.This structure leverages a particularly important moment in the player journey: the point at which the player wants to continue playing but has exhausted the resource required to do so .
Because Energy is directly tied to the core gameplay loop, the offer appears at a highly relevant moment. Players are not purchasing an abstract resource; they are purchasing the ability to keep tapping, merging, completing orders, and progressing.
The game also offers bundles that include Energy alongside additional resources, creating a broader monetization layer for players who are looking for more value than a simple Energy refill. But the depth of Energy monetization in Merge 2 deserves an article of its own.
Producer Cooldowns: Another Layer of Friction
Energy is not the only system controlling the pace of item generation. Some Producers also use a cooldown mechanic .
After producing a certain amount of items, a Producer becomes temporarily unavailable. Cooldown duration varies between Producers, and players can either wait for the Producer to recover or spend Gems to skip the cooldown.
This creates a second resource gate that operates alongside Energy. While Energy limits how much players can produce , cooldowns can limit when they can produce it .
From a retention perspective, cooldowns introduce another natural return point: players have a reason to come back once a valuable Producer becomes available again.
From a monetization perspective, they create another opportunity at a moment of high player intent. Players who are deeply engaged in a session may prefer to spend Gems rather than interrupt their momentum and wait.
Social
In terms of social features, there are currently several available, most of which are based on competition between players. Examples of existing features include a point-accumulation tournament (where points are earned by completing orders), a race where the first player to collect a certain amount of coins wins, Lava Quest, Duel, Partner, and more.
At the same time, the genre is increasingly exploring cooperative social experiences. Tasty Travelers recently introduced a cooperative event in which players team up with an ally to complete orders together and earn rewards. While cooperative mechanics such as Partners are already established within the genre, these implementations demonstrate the broader opportunity to create more meaningful forms of collaboration and social engagement.
There is still a lot of potential for additional social events and features within the genre. Features like these can significantly increase engagement and emotional attachment to the game, making them an important part of the overall experience.
Some successful concepts that could work well include introducing Teams and creating more player-to-player interactions, such as sending gifts, trading items with friends at certain levels, and, of course, trading missing cards.

Written by Yael Halevi, aka Merge Queen and casual games strategist, bringing you insights shaped by years of professional Game Design experience and learnings from smash merge hits like Travel Town. 


For years, I’ve been following the gaming industry, and one of my favorite things to track is new game releases.

New games do more than just introduce new competitors. They often predict future trends, bring innovation, and show off creative mechanics. Most importantly, they give me insights into what the "next big thing" might be.

I invite you to follow me here! I’ll be sharing bite-sized, insightful posts about interesting new games, why they matter, and my personal take on them.This past May brought us several intriguing titles. However, one that truly stands out is Just Desserts, a new soft-launch title from Chinese gaming giant Century Games, better known for the most successful strategy games, Whiteout Survivals & Kingshot.

Merge 2 Crash Course

For those unfamiliar with the Merge genre, here is a quick catch-up: this genre has skyrocketed in popularity over the last few years, becoming the 2nd highest-grossing in the casual genre after match-3. Furthermore, it has shown phenomenal year-over-year growth, and it’s not slowing down anytime soon.

Right now, the undisputed king of the genre is Gossip Harbor (from Chinese Microfun), which has comfortably cemented its spot as one of the Top 5 highest-grossing mobile games globally. 

To give you a quick, no-nonsense crash course on how we got here: Gossip Harbor actually started as a game heavily inspired by Love & Pies (from Trailmix, a Supercell studio). But in a classic student-surpasses-the-master twist, it outworked and evolved into a fierce competitor that has left everyone else in the dust.

But market growth alone doesn’t explain why Merge 2 has become such a powerful genre. To understand what makes these games so engaging, and why the formula has proven so scalable, we need to look under the hood at the core gameplay loop that drives the experience.

The Core Gameplay Loop

The core gameplay loop takes place on a board filled with Producers and orders that give players clear goals to work toward. Players tap Producers to generate items, then merge two items of the same type to progressively reach the items required by orders. Each tap consumes Energy, making it the resource that powers the core loop.Completing these orders rewards players with resources, enables progression, and ultimately allows them to renovate and develop the Meta, the space where the game’s narrative unfolds.

While the board provides the moment-to-moment gameplay, the Meta and its narrative give that gameplay a larger purpose. Players are not simply merging items for the sake of merging, they are completing orders for the characters they have become invested in, using their progress to unlock new areas, advance the story, and see what happens next.The interesting part is that the merge loop doesn’t exist in isolation. While the board provides the actions that keep players busy, the Meta gives those actions meaning. This connection between gameplay and narrative is one of the key reasons Merge 2 games can turn a relatively simple mechanic into such a sticky experience.

Narrative as a Retention Driver

Narrative plays a critical role in the overall experience and is one of the key drivers bringing players back to the game. This is particularly relevant in the Merge 2 genre, where the majority of the audience is female and emotional investment in characters can become a powerful engagement driver.

Love & Pies is one of the strongest examples of this approach. The game established a highly engaging cast of distinctive characters and built a compelling narrative around them, helping it achieve exceptionally strong retention within the genre. Its approach to character-driven storytelling has since become an important benchmark for many Merge 2 titles that followed, including Gossip Harbor.

Importantly, the narrative characters are not disconnected from the core gameplay. They are also the characters requesting orders on the board. This creates a direct relationship between the two layers of the game: the characters provide the motivation, while the board provides the activity through which players help them. Players are effectively “working for” these characters, transforming each merge and completed order into a small contribution toward the larger story.

The “One More Merge” Effect

A major part of what makes the Merge 2 loop so compelling is the perception of constant, achievable progress.

Every order is broken down into smaller merging steps, creating a clear path toward completion. As players get closer to the requested item, the goal feels increasingly attainable- often creating the feeling that they are “just one more merge” away.

This creates a powerful progression illusion: the player is continuously moving forward, but there is always another small step within reach. That combination of visible progress, achievable goals, and incomplete tasks makes disengagement surprisingly difficult.

The board itself reinforces this behavior. Players are constantly balancing several micro-goals at once as they find themselves caught in an almost endless OCD-like loop: generating items, merging, completing orders, freeing up board space, and organizing their inventory. This creates a highly satisfying optimization loop in which players naturally want to “clean up” the board before stopping.

In other words, the game is not only asking players to progress,it is constantly giving them something that feels almost finished.

Energy: The Resource Powering the Economy

At the center of the game economy is Energy, the primary resource governing item generation.

Players spend Energy by tapping Producers, with one tap costing one Energy. This creates a direct relationship between the core gameplay action and the game’s primary resource economy: the more players want to merge and progress, the more Energy they need to generate items.

Energy regenerates automatically at a rate of one Energy every two minutes, with a maximum capacity of 100 Energy. As a result, a fully depleted player can naturally refill their Energy in approximately 3 hours and 20 minutes.

This creates a built-in return loop. Players who want to maximize their free Energy have a clear incentive to return several times throughout the day, turning resource regeneration into a lightweight but effective retention mechanism.

Energy as a Monetization Lever

Energy not only regulates gameplay, but it also creates one of the game’s most important monetization opportunities.

Once players run out of Energy, they are presented with the option to purchase additional Energy using Gems. The cost increases with successive purchases, starting at 10 Gems, followed by 20 Gems, then 40 Gems, and so on. Importantly, the Energy purchase ladder resets daily, making it more than a one-off monetization opportunity: it becomes part of the player’s daily resource routine.

Personally, I find this to be one of the game’s more powerful “slippery slope” monetization areas. The individual purchases feel small and easy to justify; 10, 20, or even 40 Gems can feel like such a low commitment that I barely register them as a meaningful purchase. Yet because the ladder resets every day, these small decisions can quickly become part of my daily routine.

This is one of the few games where I genuinely feel that I have very little resistance to making these small, recurring purchases. The game almost smoothly and subtly nudges me into spending, without any single purchase feeling significant enough to trigger a strong sense of friction. This is a strong example of the foot-in-the-door effect: the first, relatively small purchase lowers the psychological barrier to spending, making the next purchase feel more acceptable, and so on. 

That makes the Energy system particularly interesting from a monetization perspective: the strength is not necessarily in the size of the purchase, but in how effortlessly the game turns spending into a habit.This structure leverages a particularly important moment in the player journey: the point at which the player wants to continue playing but has exhausted the resource required to do so.

Because Energy is directly tied to the core gameplay loop, the offer appears at a highly relevant moment. Players are not purchasing an abstract resource; they are purchasing the ability to keep tapping, merging, completing orders, and progressing.

The game also offers bundles that include Energy alongside additional resources, creating a broader monetization layer for players who are looking for more value than a simple Energy refill. But the depth of Energy monetization in Merge 2 deserves an article of its own.

Producer Cooldowns: Another Layer of Friction

Energy is not the only system controlling the pace of item generation. Some Producers also use a cooldown mechanic.

After producing a certain amount of items, a Producer becomes temporarily unavailable. Cooldown duration varies between Producers, and players can either wait for the Producer to recover or spend Gems to skip the cooldown.

This creates a second resource gate that operates alongside Energy. While Energy limits how much players can produce, cooldowns can limit when they can produce it.

From a retention perspective, cooldowns introduce another natural return point: players have a reason to come back once a valuable Producer becomes available again.

From a monetization perspective, they create another opportunity at a moment of high player intent. Players who are deeply engaged in a session may prefer to spend Gems rather than interrupt their momentum and wait.

Social

In terms of social features, there are currently several available, most of which are based on competition between players. Examples of existing features include a point-accumulation tournament (where points are earned by completing orders), a race where the first player to collect a certain amount of coins wins, Lava Quest, Duel, Partner, and more.

At the same time, the genre is increasingly exploring cooperative social experiences. Tasty Travelers recently introduced a cooperative event in which players team up with an ally to complete orders together and earn rewards. While cooperative mechanics such as Partners are already established within the genre, these implementations demonstrate the broader opportunity to create more meaningful forms of collaboration and social engagement.

There is still a lot of potential for additional social events and features within the genre. Features like these can significantly increase engagement and emotional attachment to the game, making them an important part of the overall experience.

Some successful concepts that could work well include introducing Teams and creating more player-to-player interactions, such as sending gifts, trading items with friends at certain levels, and, of course, trading missing cards.
